claims.text: Intentionally promoting coherent nanoprecipitates in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings improves wear resistance.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces relieve stress concentrations that can cause premature crack initiation.
Relieving local stress concentrations reduces microcrack initiation specifically during sliding wear.
Conventionally processed refractory high-entropy-alloy coatings typically have an unoptimized distribution of nanoprecipitates or second-phase particles.
A controlled thermal treatment or adjusted processing parameter can produce uniformly distributed, coherent nanoprecipitates in the coating.
The relevant structural mediator is a uniform distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates that interacts with dislocations during deformation.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion.
The interaction of dislocations with coherent nanoprecipitates promotes controlled transmission rather than abrupt stress localization.
Reduced microcrack initiation decreases material removal during sliding wear.
Treated coatings with controlled coherent nanoprecipitates should have a lower wear rate than baseline coatings.
Treated coatings should have a lower microcrack density near the wear interface than baseline coatings.
Omitting the targeted treatment produces a less coherent or more heterogeneous precipitate distribution.
The proposed mechanism should apply to refractory high-entropy-alloy protective coatings from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
Plastic-deformation mechanisms dominate coating wear over the proposed ambient-to-moderately-elevated temperature range.
Direct wear-performance data linking precipitate coherence to wear mechanisms in these alloys is limited.
The magnitude of wear improvement and its scaling with nanoprecipitate volume fraction and size are uncertain.
A statistically significant reduction in wear rate is required for the treated coating to satisfy the predicted outcome.
